sections.h2: Where is the Livingston County Register of Deeds office?
sections.html:
The office sits in the Historical Courthouse at 200 E Grand River Ave, Howell, the county seat. Call (517) 546-0270. The counter opens weekdays at 8:00 a.m. and shuts at 4:30 p.m., with county holidays off.

Most documents never reach the counter. Title companies and attorneys send them electronically through four certified vendors: CSC, ePN, Indecomm and Simplifile. A few instruments cannot go that way, including deeds that come with valuation affidavits, plats, and master deeds with large drawings. Those must be brought in or mailed on paper.

Livingston County sits in southeast Michigan along I-96, US 23 and M-59, with 585 square miles of area and a 2020 census population of 193,866. Roughly 86 percent of occupied homes belong to their residents, which keeps deeds flowing through this office steadily. The Census Bureau counted Brighton, Howell and nearby South Lyon as one contiguous urbanized area, and employers such as Tribar, PepsiCo and Citizens Insurance anchor the local economy. Sellers outside those towns, in the rural townships, record at the same counter. The county is laid out in 16 townships of 36 one-mile sections each, which is why legal descriptions on a Livingston deed read as a section number plus a starting corner.

sections.h2: Which fees does the Livingston County office charge?
sections.html:
Every recording carries a flat $30.00 charge, and $4 of it is sent to the Michigan State Survey and Remonumentation fund. If one instrument assigns or discharges several earlier records, each reference past the first adds $3.

Livingston County Register of Deeds fee schedule from the county FAQ
ServiceFee
Recording a document$30.00 flat
Each extra liber and page cross-reference$3.00
Tax certification, first 25 parcel numbers$5.00, then $0.20 per added number
Fixture filing$30 per document
Copy of a recorded page$1.00 ($2.00 for plat or condo drawings)
Certifying a copy$5.00, all pages must be bought
Tract index use, unless it is your own property$10 per hour

Recording fees and transfer tax are never put on a charge account. Pay with cash, check or card; a card adds a service fee.

sections.h2: How does the office calculate transfer tax?
sections.html:
If a deed states a price, the office takes transfer tax the moment it records. The county describes the total as .086 of the amount, meaning $8.60 per $1,000: $1.10 per $1,000 to the county and $7.50 per $1,000 to the state. The grantor normally bears it. Before the math, the price rounds up to the next $500 step, so $100,000.01 is treated as $100,500.

Applied to a $300,000 price, the total is $2,580. Land that straddles two counties needs the price divided by county on the deed itself.

Exemptions exist. A deed may be exempt from the state share alone or from both shares, never from the county share by itself, and the exemption cited must fit the facts on the page. Mistakes the office sees:

  • Claiming the family-gift exemptions when a trust is the grantor; an individual has to be the grantor.
  • Assuming a church is automatically exempt.
  • Assuming a sheriff's deed escapes county tax. It is always exempt from the state portion, but exempt from the county portion only when the mortgage is federally backed.
  • Citing the under-$100 exemption while the deed shows a $5,000 price.

sections.h2: What does a tax certification cover?
sections.html:
A tax certification is a Treasurer's sticker showing that taxes are paid up and that the legal description matches the township tax roll. It is part of what makes a warranty deed a warranty deed. The county requires it before recording warranty deeds, any deed with "warrant" in the conveyance line, land contracts, assignments of land contract (except those given as collateral), master deeds, and master deed amendments that add property to a condominium.

For a mailed document, enclose the $5.00 and the office gets the certification for you. An e-recorded document that needs one goes through the document router so both departments receive it. The county treasurer's page lists tax clearance of deeds among its duties, so a seller with unpaid taxes learns of it at this stage at the latest.

sections.h2: How do copies, searches and corrections work here?
sections.html:
Searching the index by name is free online. Viewing a page costs $1 plus a convenience fee that covers card processing, and a link arrives immediately. Certified copies, death certificates, tax liens, condo master deeds and documents over 75 pages are mailed after purchase. Records are imaged and indexed back to November 7, 1980 (liber 1000), with earlier books imaged or kept in hard copy.

  • You cannot change a signed, notarized or recorded deed. Adding or removing a name takes a new deed signed by the current owners.
  • When a joint tenant or spouse dies, recording the death certificate shows the survivor as sole owner without a new deed.
  • An enhanced life estate (ladybird) deed becomes proof of ownership once both death certificates are recorded.
  • Paying off a mortgage produces a discharge, not a new deed.
  • A rejected document comes back with a letter listing the reasons, and it can be corrected and resubmitted.

Paper filings by mail or at the counter must come with a return envelope or $3 for postage. Giving an email address instead brings the recorded copy back at no charge, usually the same day.

sections.h2: Can the Livingston County office tell me when my house was built?
sections.html:
No. Deeds describe land and a legal description and rarely say whether a building stood on it, so the office points owners to the city or township assessor. The Howell Carnegie Library reference desk, at (517) 546-0720, can search its archives, and the county Plat Books for 1875, 1895 and 1915 show homesteads and, in 1875, the houses in the towns.

Staff offer one rough method for older homes: a deed whose price is far below a mortgage recorded the same day often marks an owner who was about to build. Name indexes go back to the first recorded documents in 1836 and 1837, and the grantor and grantee indexes reflect documents listed in the tract index. For a sale, a seller who wants proof of a renovation or a permit should ask the local building department instead.

sections.h2: What should a seller verify before the sale closes?
sections.html:
Have the closing agent pull the recorded chain: vesting deed, recorded death certificate if any, mortgage discharges and liens. The Register of Deeds says it cannot verify ownership, since unrecorded land contracts or deeds can affect it, and its staff do not run title searches or give a guarantee. Title companies do that work and can also check probate court records the recorder lacks.

Per the county Equalization Department, the buyer owes the local assessor a property transfer affidavit within 45 days or faces $5 a day in fines, up to $200, and the home's taxable value is uncapped the next year. A seller who knows the taxes will jump for the buyer can say so up front, because it affects what the buyer can afford.

Back taxes, estate paperwork and repair needs are the usual reasons owners ask for a cash sale. Recording works the same whoever the buyer is.

faqs.q: What is the Livingston County recording fee?
faqs.a: The flat fee is $30.00 per document, including $4 for the state survey and remonumentation fund. Extra cross-references cost $3 each, and transfer tax is separate.
Usually the seller, who is the grantor. It is collected at recording: $1.10 per $1,000 for the county and $7.50 per $1,000 for the state, using a price rounded up to a $500 step.

faqs.q: Can I record a photocopy of a deed?
faqs.a: No. Only documents with original signatures can be recorded, and even electronic services must scan originals. Court orders, death certificates and surveys must be certified versions.

faqs.q: How do I put a family member on my deed?
faqs.a: The current owners must sign a new deed conveying the property to everyone who should hold title. A signed or recorded deed cannot be altered, and a lawyer or title agent can draft the new one.

faqs.q: Does the office run title searches?
faqs.a: No. The office does not do title searches or furnish abstracts and cannot guarantee results. Title companies perform and insure searches, while the office teaches the public how to use its index.
